title: Goldberg v. Kelly
lead: Welfare recipients challenge cutoffs before an evidentiary opportunity, and a new written-review procedure fails to cure the immediate subsistence risk.

actors.name: Twenty New York City welfare recipients
actors.role: Plaintiffs and intervenors challenging actual or threatened termination.

actors.name: City Commissioner of Social Services
actors.role: The sole appellant among city and state defendants.

actors.name: Altagracia Guzman and Juan DeJesus
actors.role: Recipients whose disputed eligibility grounds illustrate fact and policy disputes.

proceedings: Recipients filed two actions challenging termination without prior notice or hearing.
A three-judge District Court required adequate pretermination process despite procedures adopted during suit.
The Supreme Court affirmed, leaving individual substantive eligibility undecided.
limits: The decision does not require appointed counsel, a full judicial trial, or payment through every level of review. Burger’s and Stewart’s shared dissents are preserved from the canonical brief’s comparison with Wheeler, rather than represented as new independent companion-source review.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Recipients contest threatened or completed welfare cutoffs
sections.cue: What interests and disputes brought them to court?
paragraphs: New York City welfare recipients faced actual or threatened cutoffs of their assistance. Fourteen of the twenty people later named as plaintiffs or intervenors received federally supported, state-administered Aid to Families with Dependent Children, or AFDC; six received state and local Home Relief. Eligibility rules made these statutory programs, not discretionary gifts.
Altagracia Guzman disputed whether she had to cooperate in suing her estranged husband. Juan DeJesus denied the drug use underlying an official demand for counseling and rehabilitation.

The recipients brought two consolidated actions, alleging that payments had been or would be stopped without prior notice and a hearing. At filing, no advance notice or hearing was required. Some plaintiffs later had hearings or resumed payments, but unresolved eligibility disputes and termination threats persisted. The Court did not finally determine that every claimant was eligible.

sections.title: The city adopts written review while litigation proceeds
sections.cue: Why did a later full hearing remain inadequate?
paragraphs: The new procedure began with a caseworker discussing eligibility doubts, then sending a termination recommendation to a supervisor. If approved, a letter explained reasons and allowed seven days to request higher-official review. Recipients could submit written statements personally or with help. If the higher official upheld termination, payments ended with another explanatory letter.

Recipients could not appear before that official, present oral evidence, or confront adverse witnesses. After cutoff, an independent state officer could hold a full fair hearing with appearance, evidence, confrontation, cross-examination, and a record. Successful recipients recovered withheld benefits; unsuccessful ones could seek state judicial review. The later hearing’s own validity was not challenged. The question was whether it justified stopping subsistence aid before any evidentiary opportunity.

A three-judge District Court held that it did not. Only the city’s Commissioner of Social Services appealed, although state officials also were defendants. He accepted that due process applied but disputed the required timing and form.

sources.pinpoint: Assistance procedures; Litigation; 397 U.S. at 258–264 & nn.5–7

sections.title: Brennan treats immediate subsistence as decisive to timing
sections.cue: Why could repayment not fully repair an erroneous cutoff?
paragraphs: Justice Brennan’s majority rejected excluding statutory benefits from constitutional protection by calling them privileges. Qualified recipients held entitlements, and state termination adjudicated important interests. The opinion related those interests to other government-created forms of security such as unemployment benefits, exemptions, and public employment.

Required process depended on governmental function, the severity of loss, and the interest in prompt action. These payments supplied food, clothes, shelter, and medical care to people ordinarily without independent resources. Cutting them off could produce desperation and undermine the ability to challenge the decision. Later repayment restored money but could not provide necessities during the gap.

Government also benefited from accurate decisions and avoiding wrongful exclusion. The Commissioner invoked fiscal conservation, hearing costs, and many unchallenged terminations. The majority recognized both expense and difficulty recovering interim payments from ineligible, judgment-proof recipients. It nevertheless gave greater weight to subsistence and preventing error, noting that prompt hearings and efficient use of staff could reduce burdens.

sources.pinpoint: Entitlement and immediate loss; 397 U.S. at 262–266 & nn.8–12

sections.title: The Court requires an informal but effective opportunity before cutoff
sections.cue: Which protections were essential, and which were not required?
paragraphs: Because a full fair hearing remained available, the preliminary hearing could focus on checking the agency’s grounds. It needed no complete record, comprehensive opinion, or judicial formality. Continuing payment through the full hearing was an alternative to holding two proceedings.

Notice had to be timely and adequate. The Court found no inherent defect in the caseworker conference and letter and did not hold seven days invariably insufficient; circumstances could demand more. The omissions were oral presentation to the deciding official and the ability to confront and cross-examine adverse witnesses and test evidence.

Many recipients could not write effectively or obtain help, and a fixed written statement could not respond to a decisionmaker’s concerns. Credibility required testing. Relaying the recipient’s account through the same caseworker who gathered adverse facts was insufficient. The Court reserved process for a purely legal dispute without contested facts.

Recipients could retain counsel, but government-appointed counsel was not required. Decisions had to rest on hearing evidence and governing law, with reasons and identification of evidence but no formal findings or full opinion. The official had to be impartial: some earlier involvement was permissible, but participation in the determination under review was not.

sections.title: Three dissenting writings contest constitutionalizing the procedure
sections.cue: What consequences were predictions rather than holdings?
paragraphs: Justice Black dissented and viewed the payments as conditional assistance rather than property requiring continuation while eligibility was disputed. More broadly, he regarded balancing humane procedure as legislative policymaking untethered to written constitutional allocation. He feared unrecoverable payments, demands for appointed counsel and continued aid through judicial review, and slower initial eligibility investigations keeping needy people off the rolls. The Court did not require those predicted extensions.

Chief Justice Burger, joined by Black, dissented in both this case and Wheeler v. Montgomery. He favored administrative experimentation, pointing to evolving federal AFDC regulations that already offered protections beyond the minimum ordered here. Rigid constitutional procedures could impede improvements or consume funds. He asked about reductions, denied increases, initial applications, and special aid, which this decision did not resolve.
Justice Stewart’s short dissent also applied to both cases. He found the issue close but considered the existing New York and California termination procedures adequate.

sources.pinpoint: Three dissenting writings; 397 U.S. at 271–279,282–285; canonical brief’s Wheeler companion-source account

sections.title: Affirmance establishes process rather than eligibility
paragraphs: On March 23, 1970, Brennan, Douglas, Harlan, White, and Marshall supported affirmance; Black, Burger, and Stewart dissented, with eight Justices then serving. The District Court’s requirement of constitutionally adequate pretermination process stood.

The recipients won protection against losing subsistence assistance before a meaningful evidentiary opportunity. They did not receive a Supreme Court determination of everyone’s eligibility or a damages award, and the judgment supplied no later resolution of the individual welfare disputes.
